title: 2027: Court gives Atiku 7 days to serve suit challenging Tinubu’s eligibility on APC
description:
By Ikechukwu Nnochiri







The Federal High Court sitting in Abuja on Wednesday issued an order for President Bola Tinubu to be served, within seven days, with the suit seeking to stop him from contesting the 2027 presidential election over his alleged submission of forged certificates to the Inde
content:
By Ikechukwu Nnochiri

The Federal High Court sitting in Abuja on Wednesday issued an order for President Bola Tinubu to be served, within seven days, with the suit seeking to stop him from contesting the 2027 presidential election over his alleged submission of forged certificates to the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC).

The court, in a ruling delivered by Justice Inyang Ekwo, approved substituted service of the legal process on President Tinubu through his political party, the All Progressives Congress (APC).

Justice Ekwo made the order after hearing a motion moved by Atiku’s lawyer, Mr. Olanrewaju Omotayo-Ojo, who stood in for Mr. Silas Onu, said to be bereaved.

The suit, marked FHC/ABJ/CS/1888/2026, was brought before the court by a former Vice President and presidential candidate of the African Democratic Congress (ADC), Alhaji Atiku Abubakar.

While the ADC was joined as the 2nd plaintiff, President Tinubu, the APC, and INEC were listed as the 1st to 3rd defendants, respectively.

Specifically, Atiku, in a 25-paragraph affidavit he personally deposed to in support of the suit, alleged that President Tinubu submitted a bogus National Youth Service Corps (NYSC) discharge certificate to INEC in support of his qualification for the presidential seat.

Insisting that President Tinubu gave false information about himself in the Form CF0001 he submitted to INEC, the plaintiffs drew the court’s attention to the fact that the NYSC certificate he submitted to the electoral body bears the name “Tinubu Bola Adekunle.”

“I know that the NYSC certificate is clearly not one obtained by the 1st defendant, as it belongs to one Adekunle.

“The said NYSC certificate, bearing the name Tinubu Bola Adekunle, is herein attached and marked as Exhibit P2.

“I know that the said NYSC certificate is still in existence and in the custody of the 3rd defendant (INEC), and that it is a forgery, as the 1st defendant’s name is not Adekunle, and yet he submitted it to the 3rd defendant to be acted upon as genuine,” Atiku averred.

He told the court that Tinubu had been parading the forged certificate since 1999, when he contested the Lagos State governorship election.

Atiku therefore urged the court, among others, to determine: “Whether, in view of the limitations in section 138(1)(a) & (b) of the Electoral Act, 2026, and section 285(14)(c) of the Constitution of the Federal Republic of Nigeria, 1999 (As Amended), the Plaintiffs will not be allowed to enforce the binding provision of section 137(1)(j) of the Constitution of the Federal Republic of Nigeria, 1999 (As Amended), which applies, mutatis mutandis, to all candidates aspiring to the office of President of the Federal Republic of Nigeria.”

As well as: “Whether the 1st and 2nd Defendants should be disqualified for presenting a forged NYSC certificate to the 3rd Defendant for the 2023 and 2027 Presidential Elections, in breach of section 137(1)(j) of the Constitution of the Federal Republic of Nigeria, 1999 (As Amended).”

Upon a positive determination of the legal questions, the plaintiffs sought a “declaration that the 1st Defendant presented a forged certificate to the 3rd Defendant when he contested for Governor of Lagos State in 1999, and thereby breached the provision of section 137(1)(j) of the Constitution of the Federal Republic of Nigeria, 1999 (As Amended).”

Likewise: “An order disqualifying the 1st and 2nd Defendants from participating in the 2027 Presidential Election, for presenting a forged certificate to the 3rd Defendant when the 1st Defendant contested for Governor of Lagos State in 1999.”

The court had earlier slated September 28 to commence full-blown hearing of the case.

The INEC has since filed processes challenging the competence of the suit, which it urged the court to dismiss.

However, it appears two Senior Advocates of Nigeria (SANs) may be on a collision course over who was briefed to represent President Tinubu in the matter.

Even though the plaintiffs had insisted on effecting personal service of the suit on President Tinubu, a former Attorney General of the Federation and Minister of Justice, Chief Akin Olujinmi, SAN, and a former President of the Nigerian Bar Association (NBA), Chief Wole Olanipekun, SAN, have separately filed processes for the 1st defendant.

The two senior lawyers separately challenged the competence of the suit and Atiku’s locus standi (legal right) to query the credentials Tinubu submitted to INEC, citing provisions of Section 29(5) of the Electoral Act 2026.

In a counter-affidavit filed on Tinubu’s behalf, Chief Olujinmi, SAN, contended that Atiku’s case had become statute-barred, noting that the certificates were submitted to INEC before August 1 and the 14-day period allowed for such litigation had elapsed.

Besides, he argued that Atiku, being a member of the ADC, has no legal right to challenge what was done by the APC.

Likewise, Chief Olanipekun, SAN, who also identified himself as Tinubu’s lawyer, filed both a preliminary objection and a counter-affidavit seeking dismissal of the suit, which he maintained is incompetent and a gross abuse of court process.

In a letter dated September 10, addressed to the Deputy Chief Registrar of the court, Chief Olanipekun, SAN, said he had been briefed by President Tinubu to lead a team of counsel to represent and defend his interests in the matter.

The letter, a copy of which was sighted by Vanguard on Wednesday, read in part:
“On or about 14th August, 2026, the public was inundated with news reports of not just the filing of the action, but also narratives of the issues purportedly submitted for the court’s consideration by the plaintiffs.

“Despite this, our client has not been served with the originating processes till date. When our client got wind that the matter would be coming up for mention before the Honourable Court on 1st September, 2026, he instructed us to appear for him, pursuant to which a member of his legal team, Prince Omosanya Popoola, SAN, appeared in court, not only to represent him, but also to collect the processes filed by the plaintiffs on his behalf, as per his instruction.

“The appearance of Prince Omosanya Popoola, SAN, on the said day is on the court’s record. Surprisingly, the plaintiffs’ counsel objected to this harmless but very reasonable application by counsel to collect the processes in open court.

“To date, our client remains the only party that has not been served with the originating processes. Further to the foregoing, we hereby (on our client’s instruction) formally apply that the court provide us with either the service copy (of the originating processes) meant for our client or a certified true copy of the said originating processes, to enable the immediate filing of his response to the plaintiffs’ suit.

“This is not only in furtherance of his right to a fair hearing, but also in demonstration of the fact that our client has nothing to hide.
“Kindly bring this letter to the urgent attention of the Honourable Presiding Judge.

“We undertake to pay the necessary fees for the certified true copies,” the letter added.

The plaintiffs have also applied to be allowed to effect some amendments to the suit, especially to change the name of the INEC form that President Tinubu allegedly attached the forged certificates to, which was wrongly referred to as Form CF001 instead of Form EC9.

title: 10 Things To Know About Olu Jacobs
description: From the stages of Britain to the heart of Nollywood, Olu Jacobs built a career that spanned more than five decades and generations of audiences.Beyond the iconic roles, commanding voice, and unforgettable presence was an actor whose journey helped connect Nigerian theatre, television, and film to t
content:
From the stages of Britain to the heart of Nollywood, Olu Jacobs built a career that spanned more than five decades and generations of audiences.

Beyond the iconic roles, commanding voice, and unforgettable presence was an actor whose journey helped connect Nigerian theatre, television, and film to the wider world.

Here are 10 things to know about the life and legacy of one of Nigeria’s most celebrated actors whose death was announced on September 16, 2026.

1. He was born in Kano State

Oludotun Baiyewu Jacobs was born on July 11, 1942, in Kano, although his roots are in the Egba Alake community of Abeokuta, Ogun State.

He was born on July 11, 1942, and is an indigene of Ogun State but spent his early life in Kano, schooled in Holy Trinity and was a member of the debating and drama societies where his interest in acting began.

2. Hubert Ogunde inspired him

He was inspired to take a shot at acting when he attended a performance by legendary Nigerian theatre practitioner Hubert Ogunde, which strengthened Jacobs’ decision to pursue acting professionally.

3. He trained in London

Olu Jacobs traveled abroad to study drama and studied at the Royal Academy of Dramatic Art (RADA) in London, one of Britain’s leading drama schools.

4. He had a British TV career

Before becoming a Nollywood icon, he appeared in British television productions including The Goodies, The Dogs of War, The Professionals and The Tomorrow People.

5. He appeared in international films

His film credits included The Dogs of War (1980), Baby: Secret of the Lost Legend (1985) and Roman Polanski’s Pirates (1986).

6. He became a Nollywood institution

Over a career spanning more than five decades, Jacobs appeared in hundreds of theatre, television and film productions.

7. Kings became his signature roles

His commanding voice and presence made him particularly memorable as kings, chiefs, traditional rulers and patriarchs.

8. He won major acting honours

Jacobs won several awards in his lifetime for his acting skills. In 2007, he won the Africa Movie Academy Award for Best Actor in a Leading Role and received other major industry honours, including the MAA Lifetime Achievement Award in 2016 and Nigeria’s national honour of Member of the Order of the Federal Republic (MFR) for his long service in the film industry.

9. He and Joke Silva built together

His marriage to fellow veteran actress Joke Silva became both a personal and professional partnership. Together, they founded the Lufodo Group and Lufodo Academy of Performing Arts.

10. His legacy goes beyond acting

From the British stage to international cinema and Nollywood, Olu Jacobs’ career connected theatre, television and film across generations, helping shape Nigeria’s modern acting tradition.

The African Democratic Congress (ADC) has described Nigeria as a traumatised country that needs experienced political leaders such as its presidential candidate, Atiku Abubakar, to steer the country through its current challenges.

Bolaji Abdullahi, the party’s National Publicity Secretary, made the submission on Tuesday during an interview with News Central, while defending the choice of Atiku and former Rivers State governor, Rotimi Amaechi, as the party’s presidential and vice-presidential candidates for the 2027 election.

Abdullahi was responding to questions about how the ADC ticket differed from the ruling All Progressives Congress (APC), particularly with both Atiku and Amaechi having previously held public offices.

He argued that holding political offices in the past should not automatically disqualify anyone from seeking office again, saying Atiku’s experience could be particularly useful given Nigeria’s current condition.

He likened Nigeria’s situation to that of South Africa after the end of apartheid, when the African National Congress (ANC) chose Nelson Mandela, despite the presence of younger politicians within the party.

“There were younger people within the African National Congress, but for a nation that had been traumatised, the party recognised that it needed someone of a father figure, someone with experience, with maturity,” Abdullahi said.

He said the ADC considered Atiku capable of playing a similar role in Nigeria because of his political experience and understanding of the country’s history.

“For a traumatised country like Nigeria, because Nigeria has been traumatised. We’ve lost more people to terrorism, to banditry than we’ve ever lost at any other time in our history as a country,” he said.

Abdullahi also cited worsening economic conditions, arguing that Nigerians were poorer than they had been previously.

He said Atiku’s experience, combined with Amaechi’s energy, would provide what he described as the balance required to address the country’s challenges.

“You need someone with the quality of experience that Alhaji Atiku Abubakar brings. You need someone with the energy and the drive of a Rotimi Amaechi to back it up,” he said.

Four persons were killed and another injured in a fatal road crash that occurred early Wednesday on the Ibadan-Lagos route at Straight Gate, Ogun State.

The Federal Road Safety Corps (FRSC), Ogun State Sector Command, confirmed that the crash occurred at about 4 a.m. on Wednesday.

According to a statement signed by Chief Route Commander Afolabi Odunsi, Public Relations Officer, FRSC Ogun State Sector Command,

Eight persons were involved in the accident, with four male adults confirmed dead, one male adult injured and three others escaping unhurt.

Two vehicles were involved in the crash: a blue Mitsubishi Cabstar, with registration number FGE 753 XA, and an ash-coloured HOWO truck, with registration number T-695 KT.

According to the FRSC, preliminary investigation indicated that speed violation and wrong overtaking were responsible for the crash.

The Corps said the Mitsubishi driver, who was allegedly travelling at high speed, rammed into the moving truck while attempting to overtake.

It added that fatigue was also identified as a contributing factor, as the driver was reportedly fatigued during the journey.

The FRSC said its rescue team received the distress report at 4:33 a.m. and arrived at the scene at 4:39 a.m., recording a six-minute response time.

The injured victim was rescued and taken to Victory Hospital, Ogere, for medical attention, while the bodies of the deceased were deposited at the FOS Mortuary, Ipara.

The crashed vehicles were subsequently handed over to the Police Motor Traffic Division, MTD, Isara Division, for further investigation and necessary action.

Reacting to the incident, the Ogun State Sector Commander of the FRSC, Corps Commander Oludare Ogunjobi, urged motorists to avoid speeding, fatigue and unsafe overtaking, particularly during early-morning journeys.

Ogunjobi advised drivers embarking on long-distance trips to get adequate rest before setting out and to overtake only when it was safe and permissible.

The Sector Commander said, “Motorists must avoid speeding, fatigue and unsafe overtaking, especially during early-morning journeys. Drivers are advised to take adequate rest before embarking on long-distance trips and to overtake only when it is safe and permissible to do so.”

He further urged motorists to prioritise safety on the roads, stressing the importance of responsible driving.

The FRSC reiterated its safety message to motorists: “Drive with care. Better to be late than never.”

title: Olu Jacobs: A Life On Stage
description: Veteran Nigerian actor and elder statesman, Oludotun Jacobs, popularly known as Olu Jacobs, has died at the age of 84.His son, Olusoji Jacobs, announced the actor’s death on Instagram on Wednesday.For more than five decades, the thespian built an extraordinary career across theatre, television
content:
Veteran Nigerian actor and elder statesman, Oludotun Jacobs, popularly known as Olu Jacobs, has died at the age of 84.

His son, Olusoji Jacobs, announced the actor’s death on Instagram on Wednesday.

For more than five decades, the thespian built an extraordinary career across theatre, television and film, moving from the British stage to international cinema before becoming one of Nollywood’s most recognisable and respected faces.

His journey was one that spanned generations and crossed borders, leaving an enduring mark on Nigeria’s performing arts.

From Kano, A Calling Emerges

Born on July 11, 1942, in Kano, Jacobs traced his roots to the Egba Alake community of Abeokuta, Ogun State. He grew up in Kano, where his interest in acting began through school drama, debating activities, and church programmes.

That early interest became a serious calling after he watched a performance by legendary Nigerian theatre practitioner Hubert Ogunde. The experience deepened his fascination with the performing arts and inspired him to pursue acting professionally.

A British Stage, A Global Career

Jacobs later travelled to the United Kingdom, where he studied at the Royal Academy of Dramatic Art in London.

His training at RADA provided a strong foundation in theatre and professional acting. He went on to work with several repertoire theatres in Britain and appeared in a range of British television productions.

During the 1970s, he featured in television programmes including The Goodies, Till Death Us Do Part, The Professionals, The Tomorrow People and Barlow at Large.

His international film credits also included The Dogs of War in 1980, Baby: Secret of the Lost Legend in 1985 and Roman Polanski’s Pirates in 1986.

A Career That Spanned Generations

After establishing himself in Britain, Jacobs returned to Nigeria and became a major figure in the country’s expanding entertainment industry.

His career stretched across theatre, television and film, with appearances in hundreds of productions over the years.

In Nollywood, he became particularly renowned for portraying kings, chiefs, traditional rulers, patriarchs and other figures of authority. His deep voice, commanding presence and theatrical training combined to create a distinctive screen persona that became instantly recognisable.

Jacobs was widely regarded as part of the generation of actors who helped lay the foundations of the Nigerian film industry as it is known today.

Honours For An Enduring Career

Jacobs’ contribution to acting earned him several major honours throughout his career.

In 2007, he won the Africa Movie Academy Award for Best Actor in a Leading Role.

He was also honoured with the Industry Merit Award for outstanding achievement in acting at the 2013 Africa Magic Viewers’ Choice Awards and received the MAA Lifetime Achievement Award in 2016.

In 2011, the Federal Government conferred on him the national honour of Member of the Order of the Federal Republic in recognition of his contribution to the Nigerian arts.

Partnership Beyond The Screen

Jacobs was married to fellow veteran actress Joke Silva. Their relationship developed into both a personal and professional partnership that became one of the most prominent unions in Nigeria’s entertainment industry.

Together, they founded the Lufodo Group, with interests spanning film production, distribution, and performing arts education.

The couple also established the Lufodo Academy of Performing Arts, contributing to the training and development of a new generation of performers.

Years Away From The Spotlight

Jacobs spent his later years largely away from the public spotlight due to health challenges.

Silva disclosed in 2021 that her husband was dealing with dementia with Lewy bodies, a degenerative condition that affected his health.

“He is dealing with issues, and it has been going on for a couple of years. It is known as dementia with Lewy bodies. It is a degenerative disease that affects the brain, and it is almost like a Parkinson’s type of disease; it affects the brain so you don’t see the shaking. It affects the person,” she said.

The actor’s health also became the subject of repeated false reports about his death. In June 2024, Silva dismissed reports that he had died, saying he was alive and doing fine. His family had similarly rejected earlier death rumours.

Jacobs subsequently remained largely out of public view, while colleagues and admirers continued to celebrate his contribution to Nigerian theatre and cinema.

Legacy Written Across Generations

Olu Jacobs leaves behind a legacy that extends far beyond the characters he played on screen.

His career connected Nigeria’s traditional theatre tradition with modern film and television, while his training and experience abroad brought an international dimension to his work.

Across more than five decades, he moved between stages, screens, and generations, becoming not simply a familiar face in Nigerian entertainment, but one of the defining figures in the country’s acting tradition.

title: Artists Exit Sheeran Tour In Solidarity With Macklemore Pro-Palestinian Comments
description: The artist Finneas and three other supporting acts announced they had quit British superstar Ed Sheeran’s tour on Tuesday, after rapper Macklemore was dropped for making pro-Palestinian comments while performing.Sheeran has denied being behind the decision to remove Macklemore, saying his tour
content:
The artist Finneas and three other supporting acts announced they had quit British superstar Ed Sheeran’s tour on Tuesday, after rapper Macklemore was dropped for making pro-Palestinian comments while performing.

Sheeran has denied being behind the decision to remove Macklemore, saying his tour’s promoter was responsible.

But Finneas — a performer also famous for work with his superstar sister Billie Eilish — Irish acts Aaron Rowe and Beoga, and Lukas Graham of Denmark all posted they were quitting Sheeran’s “Loop Tour.”

While opening for Sheeran earlier this month at New Jersey’s MetLife Stadium, Macklemore shouted “Free Palestine!” and told Palestinians they were “not forgotten.”

“Macklemore coming off tour was the promoter’s decision, it was not mine,” Sheeran wrote in a lengthy Instagram post, adding that the rapper’s contract was ended by the promoter, Messina Touring Group.

According to Sheeran, venues on the tour “communicated that they would pull the shows if he was still supporting.”

The artist said he held prolonged discussions with venue managers, including Robert Kraft, owner of Boston’s Gillette Stadium and the Patriots NFL team. But he was unable to resolve the issue, he added.

Finneas has publicly advocated for Palestinians in the past. He posted Tuesday that “artists must not be silenced when they speak up for the oppressed.”

“I stand with Palestine and its people.”

Sheeran’s touring band Beoga said they were dropping out “following the silencing of Macklemore by zionist lobbies.”

“We are a traditional Irish band who never saw ourselves playing in stadiums of that size and that opportunity is not lost on us,” the group said, adding they had been friends with Sheeran for a decade and would stay so.

But “we are Irish people who understand colonialism,” Beoga said on Instagram.

“As founding members of the Irish Artists for Palestine movement, we are committed activists for justice and will continue to be.”

Irish artist Rowe similarly cited his country’s history in explaining the decision to drop out.

“As Irish people we know all too well about genocide, forced famine and violent occupation,” he wrote, also noting that Sheeran was a friend who “has changed my life.”

Yet “I cannot stand by and allow billionaires to use their position of power to silence the rightful voices of those who speak up against Israeli genocide,” Rowe said.

– ‘Strength of purpose’ –

In his post Tuesday, Sheeran had touched on his decision not to comment publicly about political subjects, notably the war in Gaza.

“I am not complicit. I have my personal views on this devastating conflict. Just because I choose not to speak publicly, it doesn’t mean I don’t care,” he said.

“Those who come to my shows do not expect a political forum. I respect Macklemore’s strength of purpose.”

On Monday, Macklemore posted that Sheeran and his team were not behind his departure from the tour.

He said that Kraft had contacted Sheeran to tell him the rapper would not be allowed on stage and alleged that Kraft had rallied other venues to demand his exclusion.

In a statement, Kraft said that Gillette Stadium would “not provide a platform for hate speech.”

Macklemore, known for hits including “Thrift Shop” and “Can’t Hold Us,” has long vocally supported Palestinians.

In 2024 he released “Hind’s Hall,” which pays tribute to Hind Rajab, a five-year-old Palestinian girl whose death sparked a wave of international outrage.

title: Public appointments should be based on competence – PRP chieftain
description:
A presidential aspirant and chieftain of the Peoples Redemption Party, Yakubu Kingsley, has said public appointments should be based on competence, integrity and accountability rather than ethnicity, religion, political affiliation or personal loyalty.
Kingsley said the principle should guide the ap
content:
A presidential aspirant and chieftain of the Peoples Redemption Party, Yakubu Kingsley, has said public appointments should be based on competence, integrity and accountability rather than ethnicity, religion, political affiliation or personal loyalty.

Kingsley said the principle should guide the appointment of public officials while ensuring equitable representation of different regions, communities, genders and generations in government.

In a statement issued on Wednesday, the PRP presidential aspirant said, “The new direction for the country should mean combining competence with equitable representation, integrity and accountability.

“The guiding principle should be simple: Merit, Integrity, Representation, Transparency and Accountability,” he said.

He said that competence should remain a key consideration in public appointments, but no region, state, community, gender or generation should be systematically excluded from national participation.

He said the Federal Character principle should also be applied transparently and measurably in governance.

“Federal character must therefore become more than a constitutional principle invoked during political arguments; it must become a transparent and measurable instrument of governance,” Kingsley said.

He proposed a framework for public appointments that would enable Nigerians to assess the geographical, professional and other dimensions of representation in government.

According to him, such a system would help reduce political accusations and counter-accusations over appointments.

Kingsley also said inclusion should extend beyond government appointments to policymaking and consultations with different sections of society.

He listed political parties, professional bodies, religious organisations, traditional institutions, civil society organisations, academia, labour, the private sector, women and youth groups, people living with disabilities, Nigerians in the diaspora and community groups among those whose views should be considered in national development.

“Inclusion has to go beyond appointments. While government must remain constitutionally neutral, particularly in matters of religion and partisan politics, it must maintain structured channels for consultation with these constituencies and draw from their knowledge, experience and reach,” he said.

He said governance should involve broader consultation with different groups so they could contribute to policymaking, monitor implementation and provide feedback.

“Governance must not be confined to Abuja or to the political class. Government must listen to the people they serve, who experience the consequences of its decisions,” he added.

Kingsley said the principle of inclusion should also apply to communities where Nigeria’s natural resources are extracted.

“Nigeria belongs to us all; therefore, the government must reflect that reality. The country is a nation of remarkable ethnic, cultural, religious, professional, political and regional diversity.

“Legitimate interests must have voices and Nigerians must have fair opportunity to contribute to the development of the nation,” he said.

He argued that communities where petroleum, gas and solid minerals are extracted should have a greater stake in development arising from those resources.

title: Maresca defends VAR officials after Man City benefit from error
description:
Manchester City boss Enzo Maresca on Wednesday expressed sympathy for VAR officials after his team benefited from a clear error in their 1-0 win against Manchester United.



Erling Haaland scored a controversial winner in the 60th minute at Old Trafford on Sunday to make it four wins out of four fo
content:
Manchester City boss Enzo Maresca on Wednesday expressed sympathy for VAR officials after his team benefited from a clear error in their 1-0 win against Manchester United.

Erling Haaland scored a controversial winner in the 60th minute at Old Trafford on Sunday to make it four wins out of four for City in the Premier League.

Haaland was initially flagged offside but VAR ruled he was being played onside by United defender Patrick Dorgu, neglecting to take account of the position of Enzo Fernandez, who was clearly offside and was interfering with play.

Refereeing body Pro Ref acknowledged an “error of judgment”, saying that the video assistant referee should have recommended an on-field review.

But Maresca spoke up for the officials ahead of Thursday’s League Cup third round match against Championship side Norwich.

“Sometimes they go for you, the decisions, sometimes they go against you,” he said. “But also it’s not easy, I think, for the VAR, for the people that are in front of the screen, and in 10 seconds, 20 seconds they have to make a decision.

“It’s not easy for them. Sometimes they make some mistakes. I make mistakes, players make mistakes, I think it’s part of our job.”

Maresca said he was unhappy with the intense focus on the offside goal following an impressive win for his team, who were reduced to 10 men when Phil Foden was sent off in the first half.

The Italian, who replaced Pep Guardiola as manager in June, reminded reporters of a controversial incident when he was Guardiola’s assistant in the 2022/23 season.

Bruno Fernandes’s goal was given despite the presence of Marcus Rashford in an offside position in a 2-1 win for United at Old Trafford.

Maresca said he was still waiting for officials to say sorry.

“Three years ago, when I was here, it happened exactly the same against Man United,” said the former Chelsea boss.

“We lost the derby there. The goal was not a regular goal, if you remember. To be honest, no one apologised. We are still waiting for the apology for that goal.

“Sometimes it happens for you, sometimes it happens against you. It’s football.”

Maresca brushed aside a question on whether he was pleased there would be no VAR in place in the early rounds of the League Cup, bringing the focus back to Sunday’s win.

“I’m pleased with the unbelievable performance from the players on Sunday,” he said. “I’m very pleased with that. Talking about one moment after that game, when we played for 70-75 minutes with 10 players, I think it’s quite poor. I think the performance was unbelievable.”

content:
The Vice-Chancellor of Bamidele Olumilua University of Education, Science and Technology, Ikere Ekiti, Prof. Andrew Omojola, has reiterated the commitment of the university management to the welfare of its retirees.

Omojola, who dismissed insinuations that the university had abandoned its pension obligations, said, “The university is currently owing pension for August 2026 and half of July. The delay is due to paucity of funds and a technical upgrade of our payment gateway by our bankers.”

Some pensioners of the university staged a protest on Monday, September 14, over the delay in the payment of their pensions.

In a statement made available in Ikere Ekiti on Wednesday, the VC, who said the university took note of the protest, assured the pensioners that the delay was not intentional.

“This delay is not intentional. Management is working assiduously and is hopeful that payment for August 2026 will be made on or before Friday, 19th September, 2026.

“We have also planned to pay the outstanding 50 per cent of July 2026 pension within the same period to alleviate the condition of our retirees. We have maintained consistent monthly pension payments and the August 2026 delay is the first occurrence.

“For the records, the university has expended over N4 billion on pension and gratuity obligations since 2021,” Omojola stated.

He gave the breakdown of the expenditure on pension and gratuity obligations over the five-year period as death pension, N205.069m; gratuity, N570.693m; pension arrears, N165.094m; and monthly pension, N3.939bn, totalling N4.88bn.

The VC said, “Management remains sensitive to the plight of our pensioners. We acknowledge their years of service and sacrifice to the university. We assure them that their welfare remains a top priority.

“Prior to the protest, management engaged the EXCO of the retirees association and explained our current challenges. It is regrettable that this did not prevent the action taken.

“We appeal to our retirees to remain calm while we conclude payment processes. We also urge the public to disregard any information suggesting that the University has abandoned its pension obligations,” Omojola said.

content:
Business activities and vehicular movement were disrupted in Enugu, the state capital, on Wednesday as hundreds of commercial transporters and market traders took to the streets in protest against what they described as heavy taxation and rising fuel prices.

The demonstrators, comprising tricycle (keke) riders, minibus drivers and shop owners, blocked major transport hubs and roads around the popular Ogbete Main Market, Old Park and Holy Ghost axis, disrupting access to the city’s central commercial district.

The protest highlights concerns over daily levies and state tax policies, which operators said were driving them out of business amid rising fuel costs.

The agitation came despite recent statements by the Executive Chairman of the Enugu State Internal Revenue Service, Ekene Nnamani, defending the state’s tax reforms.

Speaking at a revenue sensitisation forum, Nnamani said the state’s informal-sector Internally Generated Revenue surged from less than N100m annually to N7.4bn following a technology-driven consolidation of levies.

According to the state government, the central e-ticket system, costing N36,000 annually for traders and involving daily consolidated payments for transporters, was designed to eliminate illegal road tolls and multiple-agency extortion by the Enugu State Waste Management Authority, Enugu State Environmental and Climate Change Agency and local government councils.

However, operators at the scene gave a different account. Transporters alleged that daily operational taxes had been increased repeatedly, from N350 to N1,000 per day, over the past 20 months.

“We are forced to pay exorbitant daily tickets, park fees, and heavy fines if we don’t pay before noon, all while fuel prices keep climbing. Today PMS is N1,450 per liter,” said Michael Chieze, a commercial driver at the scene. “Now there are fears they want to push us out entirely.”

As traffic congestion affected parts of the capital, police units and government representatives were deployed to the Ogbete-Holy Ghost corridor to engage with the protesters and restore public order.

title: 20 notable films starring late veteran actor Olu Jacobs
description:
Oludotun Baiyewu Jacobs, better known as Olu Jacobs, died on September 16, 2026, at the age of 84, bringing to an end a screen career that spanned British theatre and television, international cinema and Nollywood.
His son, Olusoji, announced his death, prompting tributes from politicians, entertain
content:
Oludotun Baiyewu Jacobs, better known as Olu Jacobs, died on September 16, 2026, at the age of 84, bringing to an end a screen career that spanned British theatre and television, international cinema and Nollywood.

His son, Olusoji, announced his death, prompting tributes from politicians, entertainers and fans who remembered his decades-long career and contribution to the Nigerian film industry.

Trained at the Royal Academy of Dramatic Art in London, Jacobs built a career that included international productions in the 1970s and 1980s and hundreds of Nigerian films.

Beyond acting, Jacobs worked as a producer and stage director and was a co-founder of the Lufodo Group with his wife, actress Joke Silva.

Here are 20 films that feature different stages of his career, from his early international appearances to his later Nigerian productions:

1. Ashanti (1979)

Ashanti was among the earliest films in Jacobs’ documented filmography. He played Commissioner Batak in the 1979 adventure film, which featured Michael Caine, Peter Ustinov and Kabir Bedi.

The film provides an early record of Jacobs’ work in international cinema.

2. The Dogs of War (1980)

Jacobs played a Customs Officer in The Dogs of War, the 1980 film adaptation of Frederick Forsyth’s novel.

Directed by John Irvin and starring Christopher Walken, the film follows mercenaries involved in a military operation in an unnamed African country. The production became one of Jacobs’ recognised early international screen credits.

3. Baby: Secret of the Lost Legend (1985)

Jacobs appeared as Colonel Nsogbu in Baby: Secret of the Lost Legend, an adventure film produced by Walt Disney’s Touchstone Pictures.

The film follows researchers who discover a previously unknown dinosaur species during an expedition in Africa. Jacobs’ appearance added another international production to his filmography.

4. Pirates (1986)

Roman Polanski’s Pirates featured Jacobs as Boomako.

Released in 1986 and starring Walter Matthau as Captain Red, the adventure comedy marked another international production in Jacobs’ early screen career.

5. Greatness (2007)

After his early international film appearances, Jacobs featured in the Nigerian production Greatness, playing a King.

The film is among the Nigerian titles listed in his documented filmography.

6. Smoke & Mirrors (2008)

Jacobs played Alhaji Sanni in Smoke & Mirrors, another Nigerian production in his filmography.

The role came during a period when his screen career was increasingly associated with Nigerian cinema.

7. League of Gentlemen (2009)

In League of Gentlemen, Jacobs portrayed Chief Kolade.

The 2009 film is listed among his documented acting credits.

8. Bent Arrows (2010)

Jacobs played Mr Johnson in Bent Arrows, released in 2010.

The film is among the productions that featured the veteran actor during his later career.

9. Sacred Lies (2011)

Jacobs portrayed Theodore in Sacred Lies.

The 2011 production was one of several films in which he took on supporting and character roles during the period.

10. White Chapel (2011)

Jacobs appeared as Chief Tonye in White Chapel, another 2011 production listed in his filmography.

11. Adesuwa (2012)

Jacobs played Ezomo in Adesuwa, a historical Nigerian drama directed by Lancelot Imasuen.

The film is set against the history and culture of the Benin Kingdom and centres on the story of a young woman whose life becomes connected to the political and social structures of the kingdom.

12. Potomanto (2013)

In Shirley Frimpong-Manso’s Potomanto, Jacobs played Bankole.

The Ghanaian-Nigerian thriller follows an investigation that uncovers a network involved in organ trafficking. Jacobs appeared alongside Adjetey Anang and Yvonne Okoro.

Potomanto is listed as a 2013 film in available filmography records.

13. The Antique (2014)

Jacobs played Oba Ekpen in The Antique, a Nigerian drama-adventure film.

The story follows a young woman tasked with recovering a sacred antique from a forbidden land in an attempt to save a royal heir. Jacobs starred alongside Bimbo Akintola, Gabriel Afolayan and Funsho Adeolu.

14. Bloody Ring (2014)

Jacobs portrayed Osuma in Bloody Ring, another 2014 production listed among his acting credits.

15. Oloibiri (2015)

In Oloibiri, Jacobs played Timipre in a story centred on the impact of oil exploration on communities in Nigeria’s Niger Delta.

Directed by Curtis Graham, the film featured Richard Mofe-Damijo, Taiwo Ajai-Lycett and Daniel K. Daniel.

Available filmography records list Oloibiri as a 2015 film, although some accounts have given 2016 as its release year.

16. Dry (2015)

Jacobs played the Speaker in Stephanie Linus’ Dry, a film that explores child marriage and its consequences.

The film tells the story of young girls affected by child marriage and related health and social challenges.

17. One Fine Day (2015)

Jacobs was also part of the cast of One Fine Day, a Nigerian production released in 2015, according to available filmography records.

18. The Royal Hibiscus Hotel (2017)

Jacobs played Richard in The Royal Hibiscus Hotel, appearing alongside his wife, actress Joke Silva.

Directed by Ishaya Bako, the romantic comedy follows a Nigerian chef who returns home and becomes involved in efforts to save her family’s struggling hotel.

The film was also screened at the Toronto International Film Festival and became one of Jacobs’ later recognised screen appearances.

19. Victims (2017)

Jacobs portrayed Baba Deolu in Victims, another 2017 production in his documented filmography.

20. Unveil (2017)

Unveil completes the 20-film selection and is also listed among Jacobs’ 2017 acting credits.

His wider filmography extends far beyond the 20 titles listed here.

His Nigerian screen credits alone are estimated to exceed 300 titles, although IMDb currently records 216 acting credits for the late icon.

content:
The slashing of international aid finance has already hit the fight against AIDS, tuberculosis and malaria, the head of a major health fund said Wednesday, warning of a long-term impact unless the cuts were reversed.

Peter Sands, executive director of the Global Fund to Fight AIDS, Tuberculosis and Malaria, said that the immediate fallout from the cuts had been eased by countries switching resources but that “health outcomes” would suffer in coming years.

The Global Fund invested around $5.3 billion in the 2024-26 period, according to Sands, who said the institution was waiting for World Health Organization statistics for 2025 to see the impact of the cuts on lives.

The United States, Britain and other key donors have all cut aid funding.

“There is no doubt that the reductions in external funding have had an impact on health outcomes,” Sands, a former international banker, told reporters.

“What you saw in 2025 was countries shifting resources and prioritising immediate life-saving activities,” he said.

“Treatment, in a sense, did better than prevention, because understandably people were ensuring that people who had got ill were treated,” he added.

Aid cuts by western governments will have a longer impact on battling the diseases that kill hundreds of thousands of people each year, he warned.

“We saw a de-prioritisation of some longer-term activities in terms of training, capacity development, infrastructure development,” Sands said.

“It would be very difficult to sustain further reductions in funding without an escalating impact on health outcomes.”

Sands said he was most worried about the fight against malaria, which the WHO estimates kills more than 600,000 people a year. It is the issue “that keeps me awake at night” as spending was already “inadequate”.

The Global Fund says that since 2002 its efforts have helped save 72 million lives and reduced by 65 percent the overall death rate from AIDS, tuberculosis and malaria.

“Against diseases like this, if you’re not winning, you’re losing, and we need to keep winning,” he said.

title: NCDMB promotes reading culture with fifth book event in Bayelsa
description:
The Nigerian Content Development and Monitoring Board has reiterated its commitment to promoting reading culture, intellectual development and critical thinking among Nigerians.
The Executive Secretary of the NCDMB, Engr. Felix Omatsola Ogbe, stated this at the fifth edition of the Board’s Book Read
content:
The Nigerian Content Development and Monitoring Board has reiterated its commitment to promoting reading culture, intellectual development and critical thinking among Nigerians.

The Executive Secretary of the NCDMB, Engr. Felix Omatsola Ogbe, stated this at the fifth edition of the Board’s Book Reading Programme held Tuesday at the Conference Centre of the Nigerian Content Tower, Swali, Yenagoa, Bayelsa State.

The event brought together members of the Association of Nigerian Authors, Nigerian Institute of Public Relations, Nigeria Union of Journalists, academics and university undergraduates for literary discussions and intellectual engagement.

Represented by the General Manager, Corporate Communications Division, Dr Obinna Ezeobi, Ogbe said the quarterly programme was part of the Board’s corporate policy to promote reading, learning and the continuous exchange of ideas.

He said, “Books give us the opportunity to learn from the experiences and knowledge of others, and to engage issues from different perspectives.”

The NCDMB boss added that the programme was designed to provide opportunities for participants to interact with authors and thought leaders while examining contemporary issues through literature and critical discussion.

According to him, “We bring people together to share ideas.”

Ogbe noted that the mandate of the NCDMB went beyond the oil and gas industry, stressing that the Board was also committed to building human capacity in areas that would enable Nigerians to contribute meaningfully to national development.

He said, “We support businesses, we develop institutions; we also create opportunities for Nigerians to participate meaningfully in the energy sector; we enable thought processes, and we enable people to enhance their intellectual capacities.”

He further stressed that human capital development should not be limited to technical and professional skills, but should also encompass intellectual growth and a sustained culture of learning.

“We must read widely, think critically,” he said.

The guest author, Mr Paul C. Nwabuikwu, featured at the programme with his 2025 publication, The Pain and the Promise: Insights and Fragments on Nigeria and People, Public and Personal (1990-2025).

Nwabuikwu, a veteran journalist, columnist and strategic communication professional, read excerpts from selected chapters of the book and responded to questions from participants.

Explaining his motivation for writing, he said his experience as a newspaper columnist had reinforced his belief in giving depth and context to issues in order to help readers better understand events.

“Journalism is the first draft of history,” he said.

Nwabuikwu explained that several of the issues examined in the book were reactions to events that occurred between 1990 and 2025.

He cited Nigeria’s military intervention in Liberia and Sierra Leone through the Economic Community of West African States Monitoring Group as one of the events that influenced his reflections, arguing that Nigeria derived no gain of strategic importance from the costly intervention.

On the title of the book, The Pain and the Promise, the author said it reflected the contradictions of Nigeria, where citizens experience difficulties in different aspects of their daily lives while the country continues to possess enormous potential.

Responding to a question on his use of humour in writing, Nwabuikwu described humour as “an escape valve”, saying it enabled writers to communicate sensitive issues in difficult political circumstances.

“When you are writing under a military ruler who was not famous for letting his enemies escape, you have to find a way of making your point that readers are sure of what you are saying but Oga is not annoyed enough to deal with you,” he said.

On creative writing, the author advised aspiring writers to develop their individual voices rather than imitate established writers.

“Be yourself; don’t try to write like other people,” he said, urging writers to focus on issues they are passionate about.

The NCDMB Book Reading Programme was inaugurated in August 2024, with the Senior Vice Chairman and Editor-in-Chief of Leadership Newspapers, Mr Azu Ishiekwene, as the guest author.

The second edition, held on August 25, 2025, featured former Editor of The PUNCH, Mr Dayo Oketola, while King Bubaraye Dakolo, Agada IV, was the guest author at the November 13, 2025 edition.

The fourth edition, held on April 8, 2026, featured former Director-General of the Nigerian Maritime Administration and Safety Agency and former federal lawmaker, Dr Dakuku Peterside.

The programme is aimed at promoting reading and literacy, critical thinking and intellectual engagement among authors, academics, students, media practitioners and members of the general public.

content:
Former Vice President Atiku Abubakar, Minister of Aviation and Aerospace Development, Festus Keyamo, and several Nigerian entertainers have mourned veteran actor Olu Jacobs, who died at age 84.

Jacobs’ son, Olusoji, announced his death in an Instagram post on Wednesday, describing the late actor as “The Lion of Lufodo.”

Reacting to the death in a statement posted on his X handle on Wednesday, Atiku described Jacobs as “an institution, a cultural icon and one of the finest ambassadors of our creative spirit.”

Atiku said, “I am profoundly saddened by the passing of Olu Jacobs at the age of 84. Nigeria has lost far more than a great actor; we have lost an institution, a cultural icon and one of the finest ambassadors of our creative spirit.

“For generations of Nigerians, Olu Jacobs was a familiar and commanding presence in our homes. That unmistakable voice, the dignity he brought to every role and the sheer force of his talent made him one of those rare artists who did not merely act before an audience, but became part of our collective memory.

“Long before Nollywood became a global phenomenon, Olu Jacobs was already carrying the Nigerian name with distinction. Through decades of dedication to his craft, he helped lay the foundations upon which an entire industry would rise. He gave life to our stories, dignity to our culture and inspiration to countless younger actors who followed the path he helped to clear.”

Atiku also condoled with Jacobs’ wife, actress Joke Silva, their children and the wider entertainment community.

“My heart goes especially to his beloved wife and lifelong partner, Joke Silva, their children and the entire Jacobs family. I pray that the memories of the beautiful life they shared with him will bring them strength through this painful season,” he said.

He added, “Olu Jacobs gave Nigeria his talent, his voice and a lifetime of excellence. Nigeria will remember him with pride, affection and profound gratitude. May God grant his soul eternal rest and comfort his family in this hour of grief.”

Keyamo, in a post on X, described Jacobs as a consummate actor and professional.

He wrote, “Consummate actor; quintessential professional; god of the screen and legend of the stage; role model and perfect gentleman. Olu Jacobs. Rest in peace.”

Meanwhile, several actors and entertainers also paid tribute to the late actor on social media.

Content creator Broda Shaggi wrote, “May his soul find eternal rest at the right hand of God, and may his memory live on in the hearts of all who knew and loved him.”

Actor and content creator William Uchemba said, “A life well spent, Rest Well Legend.”

Isbae U wrote, “Rest well Legend ,” while Mr Macaroni described Jacobs as a “Legend, Icon and an absolute Inspiration to us all!”

Actress Ini Edo also paid tribute, writing, “Rest well Uncle! You will forever be in our hearts ”

Jacobs was one of Nigeria’s prominent veteran actors, with a career spanning theatre, television and film.

He was also a film executive and, alongside his wife, Joke Silva, was associated with the Lufodo Group and Lufodo Academy of Performing Arts.

Born on July 11, 1942, Jacobs trained at the Royal Academy of Dramatic Art in London and appeared in several British television productions and international films before becoming a major figure in Nigeria’s film industry.

He received the Industry Merit Award at the Africa Magic Viewers’ Choice Awards in 2013 and the Africa Movie Academy Awards’ Lifetime Achievement Award in 2016. He was also conferred with the national honour of Member of the Order of the Federal Republic in 2011.

title: INEC Has Fixed The Ballot, It Has Not Fixed The Opposition
description: THE SIGNALINEC has settled the formal presidential field for the January 16, 2027 election. It has not settled the political contest behind it.The commission has confirmed 18 presidential candidates and their running mates, including President Bola Tinubu of the APC, Atiku Abubakar of the ADC, Peter
content:
THE SIGNAL

INEC has settled the formal presidential field for the January 16, 2027 election. It has not settled the political contest behind it.

The commission has confirmed 18 presidential candidates and their running mates, including President Bola Tinubu of the APC, Atiku Abubakar of the ADC, Peter Obi of the NDC, and Seyi Makinde of the APM.

That gives voters a clearer list of names. But it also exposes the opposition’s central problem: several of its most prominent figures now have separate tickets, separate parties and separate campaign interests.

The nomination process has produced candidates. It has not produced a common strategy.

The question is therefore no longer simply who has secured a presidential ticket. It is whether politicians who have already been formally presented to the electorate can still coordinate, negotiate or reconsider their positions before voting day and whether they can do so without fracturing their parties and support bases.

That tension is now visible in the renewed contact between Peter Obi and Seyi Makinde.

And that is today’s Political Signal.

THE OPPOSITION’S NEW MOVEMENT

The most significant recent development is the renewed engagement between Obi and Makinde.

The two politicians have appeared together publicly in recent days, including at the inauguration of Makinde’s APM presidential campaign office.

Their contact matters because it brings together two figures with different political assets. Obi retains a strong national profile following his performance in the 2023 presidential election. Makinde is one of the country’s most prominent governors, with influence that extends beyond his immediate party structure.

Both men have played down suggestions that a formal alliance has already been reached. They have described their engagement as consultations and discussions around national political interests.

That distinction matters. A meeting is not an alliance. A public appearance is not a coalition. Consultations do not automatically lead to a joint ticket or a common campaign.

But the timing is significant.

INEC has now confirmed Obi and Makinde as presidential candidates of different parties. Their public engagement therefore shows that the formal nomination process has not frozen the opposition’s political relationships. The ballot may list them separately, but the politicians and networks behind those tickets are still testing whether they can work together.

The conversation is also moving beyond party labels. The relevant question is not only whether the APC, ADC, NDC or APM can campaign independently, but whether the personalities and networks associated with them can find enough common ground to coordinate their efforts.

That does not make a coalition.

But it does tell us something:

The opposition’s political map is still being redrawn.

THE ATIKU QUESTION HAS NOT DISAPPEARED

Atiku remains the presidential candidate of the ADC.

Obi remains the presidential candidate of the NDC.

Makinde remains the presidential candidate of the APM.

All three are officially recognised candidates, with parties that have invested in their nominations and supporters who have begun to identify with their campaigns.

That raises the political cost of any future adjustment.

Before the final list was published, cooperation could be discussed largely as a question of who might eventually emerge as the candidate of a broader opposition arrangement. Now, any such move would require existing candidates and parties to reconsider positions that have already been formally presented to the electorate.

A candidate who withdraws or supports another would have to manage the expectations of party members, campaign officials, donors, regional supporters and voters who may already have committed themselves to that candidacy.

The question becomes:

Who is prepared to change position, and what would that change require?

It would require agreement on the candidate, the platform, the campaign structure and the distribution of political influence after the election. It would also require each politician to persuade supporters that cooperation offers a better chance of victory than a separate campaign.

That is a difficult calculation.

Each candidate has a reason to believe that his own platform can attract a significant share of the vote. Each also has an established political identity and a constituency that may resist any decision to step aside.

This is why the opposition question remains unresolved. The challenge is not simply finding a candidate with national appeal, but persuading other candidates and their supporters to accept that person as the most viable vehicle for defeating the incumbent.

AND THEN THERE IS WIKE

The political picture is further complicated by the position of Nyesom Wike.

The FCT Minister has again made clear that he supports President Tinubu’s re-election while insisting that the PDP can continue to contest governorship, National Assembly and State House of Assembly elections.

His position highlights the difference between presidential politics and other levels of electoral competition.

A politician or party may support one candidate for president while continuing to contest against that candidate’s party in legislative and subnational elections. Cooperation at the presidential level therefore does not necessarily require a complete alliance across every contest.

Wike has also rejected the suggestion that his so-called “rainbow coalition” is an arrangement with the APC. He has described it instead as a vehicle for mobilising support for Tinubu across political parties.

Whether or not that distinction satisfies other political actors, it reflects the fluid nature of the 2027 contest.

Political alliances are not necessarily following party boundaries.

Candidates may compete against one another at one level while political actors within their parties support different candidates at another. Party members may campaign for official candidates in some constituencies while backing a different presidential candidate, and political leaders may maintain their party identities while building informal networks across party lines.

Nigeria’s voters have demonstrated this kind of split-ticket behaviour before. Support for a presidential candidate does not necessarily translate into support for the same party’s candidates in governorship or legislative elections.

The labels on the ballot will therefore not tell the entire story of the political alignments behind them. Formal party structures will matter, but so will personal networks, regional calculations, local alliances and the influence of individual political leaders.

WHAT HAS ACTUALLY CHANGED?

Three things have changed.

First, the formal field is now clearer. INEC has published the presidential candidates and their running mates, giving the electorate a more definite picture of the contest.

Second, the publication of the list has raised the stakes for any future political adjustment. Candidates and parties must now weigh the organisational and political costs of campaigning separately against the possible benefits of a coordinated approach.

Third, political loyalties are becoming increasingly fluid across parties, personalities and levels of government.

The result is a contest in which formal party structures and informal political relationships may not always point in the same direction.

The next phase will therefore be less about announcing alliances than about determining whether political cooperation can produce an actual electoral structure.

A serious arrangement must be able to coordinate campaign offices, mobilise voters, raise funds, manage competing interests and present a consistent message across the country.

Without that structure, cooperation may remain symbolic.

With it, the opposition could begin to look like a serious national alternative.

THE QUESTION TO WATCH

Can the opposition convert conversations into coordination?

That means agreement on:

leadership,

platform,

party structure,

running mates,

resources,

campaign messaging,

voter mobilisation,

and ultimately who campaigns for whom.

It also means resolving what happens to the existing presidential candidates and their parties.

Would one candidate step aside? Would the parties adopt a common platform? Would the arrangement be formal or informal? Would supporters accept it? And could the coalition remain united after the election?

These questions matter because political actors may agree that the incumbent should be challenged while still disagreeing over who should lead that challenge. They may share concerns about the government but differ on economic policy, regional priorities, party structure and the distribution of power.

Until those issues are resolved, every new meeting is a signal — but not yet a settlement.

WHAT TO WATCH NEXT

Watch the Obi-Makinde relationship.

The key issue is whether their engagement remains a series of consultations or develops into a more defined political arrangement. The strongest evidence will come from joint statements, coordinated activities, shared policy positions and the response of their party structures.

Watch whether Atiku remains central to any proposed opposition arrangement.

His position as the ADC presidential candidate gives him a formal platform and a national political profile. Any serious opposition strategy would have to account for his candidacy, his supporters and the organisational strength of the ADC.

Watch whether the ADC can accommodate wider opposition interests.

Its ability to serve as a political home for different groups may determine whether it becomes the centre of a broader arrangement or remains one of several competing platforms.

Watch Makinde’s political network and whether his consultations produce a structure beyond Oyo State.

His influence will be measured not only by personal popularity but also by his ability to connect with political actors, voters and organisations across the country.

And watch Wike’s political network as the campaign develops.

His support for Tinubu could influence calculations within the PDP and other opposition circles. It may also reinforce the importance of informal networks that operate across party lines.

Most importantly, watch what politicians do, rather than what they say.

Between now and January, there will be declarations of unity, appeals for cooperation and assurances that discussions are progressing.

The evidence will be in the alliances that translate into organisation, campaign structures, voter mobilisation and votes.

BOTTOM LINE

INEC has fixed the ballot. The opposition has not yet built a campaign.

The decisive test is whether its leaders can produce one candidate or agreed strategy, a shared platform, coordinated structures, joint mobilisation and disciplined public messaging.

Until those things are visible on the ground, opposition unity is only talk.

That is today’s Political Signal.

EDITORIAL NOTE

Political Signals is an independent weekly political analysis produced for Channels Television. It examines political developments, personalities and electoral trends without endorsement of any political party or candidate. Its assessments are based on publicly available evidence and may change as events and evidence develop.

title: Trapped Commuters, Motorists Lament As Lagos-Ibadan Expressway Gridlock Worsens
description: Traffic congestion has worsened on the Lagos-Ibadan Expressway, with commuters and motorists stranded for several hours around the Kara Bridge and adjoining routes, as the ongoing bridge repairs continue to disrupt movement.The situation was further aggravated by a multiple-vehicle crash involving a
content:
Traffic congestion has worsened on the Lagos-Ibadan Expressway, with commuters and motorists stranded for several hours around the Kara Bridge and adjoining routes, as the ongoing bridge repairs continue to disrupt movement.

The situation was further aggravated by a multiple-vehicle crash involving a container-laden truck on Tuesday, leaving some commuters trapped on the road overnight and forcing others to trek long distances to their destinations.

As of Wednesday morning, traffic remained heavy around Kara Bridge, Berger, OPIC, Long Bridge and adjoining routes into Lagos, as well as Ojota, Ogba and Maryland, with motorists reporting prolonged delays.

Some commuters who left work in Lagos on Tuesday evening said they were still on the road hours later.

One commuter said he resorted to trekking from New Garage to Berger after the traffic became unbearable.

Another truck driver said he was still stuck at Ikeja at about 3 a.m Wednesday and is still on hold as he is headed to Aba after travelling through the night.

A commuter said “I am headed to Mowe and I have been trekking for over three hours.”

The prolonged congestion has also affected public transportation, with some commuters reporting difficulty getting buses to work on Wednesday morning.

The situation comes amid the Federal Government’s ongoing rehabilitation of the Kara Bridge, where deteriorating expansion joints are being replaced.

The two-week project, directed by the Minister of Works, David Umahi, began on September 8 and is scheduled to run until September 22.

The Federal Ministry of Works said the expansion joints had exceeded their service life and required replacement to improve safety and preserve the structural integrity of the bridge.

The work is being carried out in phases, with one half of the affected section closed while traffic uses the other side under traffic management arrangements. The project was initially scheduled for August but was postponed following concerns over traffic management and the potential impact on road users.

However, the reduced road capacity has made the corridor particularly vulnerable to major gridlocks whenever there is an accident or vehicle breakdown.

That vulnerability was exposed again on Tuesday when a 40-foot container truck crashed at Kara Bridge.

LASEMA said preliminary findings showed that the truck developed a mechanical fault while in motion, causing the driver to lose control and ram into six other vehicles.

The crash involved the container truck, a Toyota Hilux, an interstate bus, a Hyundai Odyssey, a Sienna, a Toyota Highlander and another Mitsubishi Hilux.

Emergency responders were dispatched to the scene at about 6:05 a.m., while LASEMA, LASTMA and the police worked to manage traffic and recover the affected vehicles.

The vehicles were subsequently removed from the carriageway with assistance from private towing operators.

However, the incident triggered severe congestion as the affected section was temporarily obstructed.

A container-laden trailer incident on Tuesday afternoon compounded the existing traffic situation caused by the bridge repairs, forcing a closure of the Lagos-bound section and affecting motorists travelling in the opposite direction.

Authorities began removing barriers around the construction area to create an alternative passage and ease movement. LASTMA and Ogun State traffic officials were deployed to manage the situation.

The resulting gridlock spread beyond Kara and Berger, with traffic also affecting connecting routes into Lagos, with congestion extending beyond Long Bridge towards Magboro and into Lagos.

The prolonged traffic also led to increased transport fares on some routes, with fares rising to as much as ₦4,000 from Berger to Oshodi, ₦3,500 from Berger to Mowe, ₦1,500 from Agege to OPIC, and ₦2,000 from Magboro to Berger.

For many road users, the consequences have gone beyond delayed journeys.

Commuters have complained of lost working hours, additional fuel expenses, increased transport fares and physical exhaustion.

Some have resorted to walking long distances to escape the traffic, while others have abandoned vehicles and sought alternative means of transportation.

The latest situation has also renewed concerns about the vulnerability of the Kara-OPIC corridor, which carries a large volume of commuters, commercial vehicles and goods between Lagos, Ogun State and other parts of the country.

The Federal Government had previously explained that the Kara repairs were necessary because the damaged expansion joints posed safety risks and could contribute to more serious structural problems if left unattended.

Traffic authorities have also been deployed along the corridor to manage diversions and prevent further obstruction.

title: Police arrest man who kidnapped grandfather in Katsina, rescue two victims
description:
The Katsina State Police Command has arrested a 22-year-old man, Sani Dikko, who allegedly conspired with two others to kidnap his grandfather and secured N3m ransom before his release.
Dikko was arrested alongside Kabir Sani, 22, and Salisu Bello, 22, during an operation by operatives of the comman
content:
The Katsina State Police Command has arrested a 22-year-old man, Sani Dikko, who allegedly conspired with two others to kidnap his grandfather and secured N3m ransom before his release.

Dikko was arrested alongside Kabir Sani, 22, and Salisu Bello, 22, during an operation by operatives of the command’s Violent Crime Response Unit along Marabar Shema Village in Dutsin-Ma Local Government Area.

The command’s Police Public Relations Officer, DSP Abubakar Aliyu, disclosed this in a statement issued on Wednesday on behalf of the Commissioner of Police, CP Ali Fage.

According to the statement, the suspects were arrested on September 12, 2026, at about 8:23pm during a confidence-building patrol based on credible intelligence.

“On 12th September 2026, at about 8:23 pm, operatives of the Command’s Violent Crime Response Unit (VCRU), while on a confidence-building patrol along Marabar Shema Village, acted on credible intelligence and successfully busted a three-man kidnap syndicate.

“The suspects were identified as: Sani Dikko, m, aged 22 – Informant, Kabir Sani, m, aged 22, Salisu Bello, m, aged 22.

“During preliminary investigation, the suspects confessed to the commission of the offence. Specifically, Sani Dikko voluntarily confessed to conspiring with the other suspects to kidnap his grandfather, one Alhaji Lawal, about three weeks ago. The victim spent 16 days in captivity before securing her release following the payment of a ₦3,000,000 ransom.”

The command said all three suspects remained in custody as investigation continued to uncover their alleged wider criminal network.

Meanwhile, the police also rescued two women abducted by bandits during an attack on Sha’iskawa Fulani Village in Kankia Local Government Area of the state.

The victims, identified as 45-year-old Assubi Rabe and 27-year-old Rabi Isyaku, were reportedly abducted at about 12:45am on September 14 by about eight armed bandits.

The police said the Kankia Divisional Police Officer swiftly mobilised operatives to the scene after receiving a distress call.

The team subsequently engaged the attackers in a gun duel, forcing them to flee into the surrounding bush.

“Due to the superior firepower of the police team, the bandits fled into the surrounding bush, allowing operatives to successfully rescue both kidnapped victims unhurt,” the statement said.

The Commissioner of Police commended the operatives for their gallantry and professionalism and reiterated the command’s commitment to sustaining operations against kidnapping and banditry in Katsina State.

CP Fage also urged members of the public to continue providing the police with timely and credible information to facilitate prompt action against criminal elements.

content:
The 2026 FIFA World Cup marked the end of international careers for several established football stars, with a number of veterans announcing their retirement from international football following the tournament.

From World Cup winners to long-serving national team captains, the list includes players from Europe, Africa and South America.

PUNCH Online takes a look at 10 notable players who have ended their international careers or announced their departure from international football following the 2026 World Cup.

1. Lionel Messi — Argentina

Argentina captain Lionel Messi announced his retirement from international football after the 2026 World Cup, where his side reached the final.

The 39-year-old remains Argentina’s record appearance-maker and leading goalscorer, with 207 caps and 125 goals. FIFA reported that Messi will make a farewell appearance for Argentina against Benin in Buenos Aires on October 6.

2. Neymar — Brazil

Brazilian superstar Neymar also brought his international career to an end after the World Cup.

The forward, who made his Brazil debut in 2010, played at four World Cups. Following Brazil’s elimination, Neymar confirmed that his international journey was over.

3. James Rodríguez — Colombia

Colombia captain James Rodríguez announced his international retirement on September 15, 2026.

The 35-year-old played at three World Cups and leaves the national team as Colombia’s all-time leader in appearances, with 131, and assists, with 43. He is also Colombia’s leading scorer at the World Cup, with six goals.

4. Manuel Neuer — Germany

Germany goalkeeper Manuel Neuer ended his international career after the 2026 World Cup.

The 40-year-old had previously retired from international football after Euro 2024 but returned to the national team for the World Cup. His Germany career included the country’s 2014 World Cup triumph.

5. Guillermo Ochoa — Mexico

Mexico goalkeeper Guillermo Ochoa also ended his international career after the tournament.

Ochoa became one of Mexico’s most recognisable players during a career that included multiple World Cup appearances. He made a brief appearance during Mexico’s 2026 campaign before receiving a farewell from teammates and supporters.

6. Riyad Mahrez — Algeria

Former Manchester City star Riyad Mahrez retired from international football after Algeria’s elimination from the 2026 World Cup.

Mahrez, who made his World Cup debut in 2014, scored twice at the 2026 tournament before Algeria were eliminated by Switzerland.

7. Édouard Mendy — Senegal

Senegal goalkeeper Édouard Mendy announced his international retirement in September.

The 34-year-old finished his Senegal career with 59 appearances and was part of the team that won the 2021 Africa Cup of Nations.

8. Iñaki Williams — Ghana

Ghana forward Iñaki Williams announced his international retirement after Ghana’s defeat by Colombia in the Round of 32.

Williams ended his four-year international career with 28 appearances for the Black Stars.

9. Edin Džeko — Bosnia and Herzegovina

Bosnia and Herzegovina captain Edin Džeko announced on September 3, 2026, that he would retire from international football.

The 40-year-old is scheduled to play his final match for Bosnia and Herzegovina against Sweden on October 2 in the UEFA Nations League.

Džeko has been one of the most important players in Bosnia and Herzegovina’s history and is the country’s record goalscorer and appearance-maker.

10. Seko Fofana — Côte d’Ivoire

Côte d’Ivoire midfielder Seko Fofana announced his retirement from international football on September 14, 2026, at the age of 31.

Fofana made 34 appearances and scored seven goals for the Elephants. He was also part of the Côte d’Ivoire squad that won the Africa Cup of Nations on home soil in 2024.

content:
Veteran Nollywood actor Olu Jacobs has died at the age of 84.

The actor’s death was announced in an Instagram post shared by his son, Olusoji Jacobs, on Wednesday, September 16.

“It is with gratitude to God for a life well lived and fought that we announce the passing of our dear husband, father, grandfather, and uncle. The Lion of Lufodo,” he wrote.

The family called on all social media bloggers and influencers to respect their privacy as they mourn.

“We call on all bloggers and social media influencers to respect our family’s privacy at this time,” he added.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Olusoji_Jacobs (@mrjacobs_jnr)

Born in 1942, Jacobs’ legendary career spanned more than five decades across the United Kingdom and Nigeria. After training at the prestigious Royal Academy of Dramatic Art (RADA) in London, his early screen credits included British television classics such as “The Goodies” and “The Professionals,” alongside international film appearances.

He worked as an actor for most of his life, returning to Nigeria in the 1980s to help pioneer the booming Nigerian film industry, Nollywood, where he built an enduring legacy playing authoritative monarchs and beloved father figures.

Behind his celebrated artistic career lay a severe personal health battle in his final years.

In 2021, his wife of nearly four decades, veteran actress Joke Silva, revealed that Jacobs had been diagnosed with Dementia with Lewy Bodies (DLB), a progressive neurodegenerative condition.

The diagnosis ended years during which the family repeatedly had to debunk false internet rumors surrounding his health.

A legacy of artistry

Throughout his later years, industry colleagues and admirers routinely reflected on the deep bond between Jacobs and his wife. Together, the couple co-founded Lufodo Group, a media and performing arts firm that helped groom generations of Nigerian creative talent.

Speaking candidly in past interviews about his cognitive decline, Silva described the emotional weight of caring for a partner facing dementia while holding on to their shared history.

“It’s been hard on him because he doesn’t understand everything that is going on, and hard on the family,” she previously shared during a television interview addressing his health. “I miss the times we worked together, but we remain deeply grateful for every clear, beautiful moment we have.”

Jacobs was conferred with the national honor of Member of the Order of the Federal Republic (MFR) in 2011 and received the Industry Merit Award at the Africa Magic Viewers’ Choice Awards.
